Fugue in C Major, BWV 545 Rhetorical

The organ fugue that Scott Roberts (2004, chapter 6) uses to show an unexpected change in the prevailing rhythm as a notable property. Four times the running eighths stop for a bar, and those bars cut the fugue into sections of 18, 36, 27 and 27 bars, ratios of the octave, fourth and unison. It is also his first case where step 4, a new segmentation, matters, and his first with entries hidden in the texture. The subject cannot step past 4 until the last three bars, where the line finally climbs from 1 to 1.

  • 111 bars, alla breve
  • 4 voices
  • 16 entries, 6 of them obscured
  • 4 sections and an extension
  • Blocked ascent reconciled

The Six Steps

As in his other organ chapters, Roberts reports the steps as a narrative; the sorting into cards is ours ours. This is the first fugue in his study where step 4 applies.

  1. STEP 1

    Identify the Traditional Fugue Elements

    Mark every entry, countersubject, codetta, episode and coda, with voice, key and devices.

    • Sixteen entries (Figure 25): the exposition alternates C and G (alto, tenor, bass, soprano); later entries visit G, C, A minor, E minor, F major and D minor.
    • Six entries are hidden, fully or in part, by the voices around them.
  2. STEP 2

    Find the Notable Properties

    Look in the subject and exposition for linear lines, patterns, suspended degrees, contrasts and structural units.

    • Static, then active: half notes, then quarters; this time the contrast is only rhythmic.
    • Blocked ascent: the subject climbs 1 to 4 and never steps on to 5.
    • Rhythmic halts: once eighths take over (m. 8), they stop unexpectedly in four bars.
  3. STEP 3

    Look for Patterns in the Sections Nothing found

    Measure the sections from step 1: do they grow, shrink, mirror or form simple ratios?

    Because so many entries are covered by the texture, the traditional sections carry little weight. Roberts calls that segmentation inconsequential here.

  4. STEP 4

    Test Other Segmentations

    Use a notable property to cut the fugue another way.

    The four bars of quarter notes, mm. 18, 54, 81 and 108(9), each fall on a cadence. Roberts treats them as pillars that divide the fugue into four sections and a cadential extension.

  5. STEP 5

    Repeat the Pattern Search

    Look for patterns again in the new segmentation.

    Lengths 18, 36, 27, 27: II to I is 2:1 (octave), II to III 4:3 (fourth), III to IV 1:1 (unison). Entries per section 4, 5, 3, 4: 5:4 (major third) and 4:3. The numbers of the last entry in each section, 4, 9, 12 and 16, give 3:2, 4:3 and 4:3.

  6. STEP 6

    Decide How the Fugue Responds

    A property is reconciled when it returns with the trait that made it notable, now completed. All reconciled: rhetorical.

    Rhetorical. In the last three bars the line climbs from 1 through 4 and 5 to 1: up the bass to 5, then on in the soprano. Roberts lists this fugue with the rhetorical ones in his overview (chapter 1).

Notable Properties

The properties Roberts finds, and what becomes of each. The buttons scroll the score to the place and play it.

Contrast

Half notes, then quarters

Why notable
The static-then-active pattern of BWV 578 and 533 returns, made by rhythm alone.
Role
It starts the rhythmic story: from half notes to quarters, to eighths by m. 8.
Blocked ascent

No step from 4 to 5

Why notable
The subject climbs C–D–E–F and reaches G only by leap. The gap between 4 and 5 runs through the subject and the material that goes with it, so it fills the fugue.
Reconciled
mm. 109–111: C–D–E–F–G in the bass, then on to C in the soprano, a complete ascent from 1 to 1.
Unexpected rhythmic change

Four bars without eighths

Why notable
Once eighths prevail they stop four times, each time at a cadence: mm. 18, 54, 81 and 108(9).
Role
These pillars give the sections whose lengths form the ratios above. This property matters most, because the hidden entries show that Bach put form ahead of making entries stand out.
Hidden material

Obscured entries

Why notable
Six entries, all in inner voices, are covered by voices above and below or by a melodic idea already under way.
Role
They make the traditional structure inconsequential, yet without them most of the ratios would not exist. Roberts suggests that hidden entries tell the analyst to look beyond the subject.

The quarter-note bars close the sections, so each section here runs through its pillar bar. Roberts gives the last as m. 108(9); in this encoding the eighths run through m. 108 and stop in m. 109, which is where the extension begins.

Obscured Entries

How an Entry Gets Hidden Roberts

An entry in the top or bottom voice is always easy to hear. To be hidden, it needs voices above and below it, and it helps if it starts in the middle of a melodic or harmonic idea that is already moving.

  • mm. 28 and 35 (tenor, alto): secondary to a line that runs from m. 19 to m. 38.
  • m. 52 (alto, A minor): under material that starts in m. 50 and cadences in m. 55.
  • m. 79 (alto): under material from m. 76 to m. 85.
  • mm. 84 and 89 (tenor, alto): only partly hidden. The bass drops out in m. 85, leaving the tenor at the bottom; the soprano rests in m. 89 and covers the alto again from m. 90.

What It Means Roberts

Bach plainly did not care whether these entries stood out. That puts the weight on form, the sections cut by the rhythmic halts, ahead of the static-active contrast and the blocked ascent, without cancelling those. Melodic and harmonic continuity comes second, since it takes precedence over the entries.

Yet the hidden entries are needed: without them most of the entry-count ratios would vanish. Roberts offers a tentative rule: when entries are obscured, look elsewhere than the subject for the important notable properties.

In the score, a bracket marked “obscured entry” sits over each one.

About This Score

Notes and Layout

The score is engraved from Peter van Kranenburg’s Humdrum encoding of BWV 545. It is the only machine-readable source found so far, so the notes are still to be checked bar by bar against the Bach-Gesellschaft edition (BG 15, 1867). Roberts quotes the Neue Bach-Ausgabe IV/5; bar numbers agree.

Each voice has its own staff (open score); Bach’s layout has two manual staves and pedal. The encoding’s mordents and trills are played. The 6 grace note in m. 110 that Roberts cites from the Neue Bach-Ausgabe is not in this encoding.

Playback uses recorded samples: the Steinway Grand by default, an Italian harpsichord at A = 415, or a baroque pipe organ at Chorton A = 465 with pedal pipes for the bass.

What Is Roberts and What Is Ours

  • Roberts The entries with voices and keys (Figure 25), the properties, the pillar bars and sections (Table 9), all ratios, the obscured entries (Figures 31–33) and the reconciling ascent (Figure 29). The rhetorical label is from his overview in chapter 1; chapter 6 does not name it.
  • ours Exact entry positions (template matching); confirming the quarter-note bars by counting onsets; the sorting into six steps; bracket placement.

Sources. Scott Roberts, Toward a Methodology for the Analysis of Fugue: An Examination of Selected Bach Organ Works, PhD diss., Florida State University, 2004, chapters 1 and 6. Encoding: Peter van Kranenburg, Humdrum edition of BWV 545 (KernScores), used for study. Reference edition: Johann Sebastian Bach, Orgelwerke II, Bach-Gesellschaft Ausgabe vol. 15 (Leipzig, 1867).
